instructions:
## The project being researched

An XGBoost "virtual sensor" for Iowa stream nitrate: predict at locations with NO physical sensor, using only weather + land-use data. Two targets:
- REGRESSION: daily-max nitrate concentration (mg/L)
- CLASSIFICATION (the primary one): binary `violation` = daily max >= 10 mg/L, base rate 0.263

~85 sensor sites, 160,074 site-days, 2008-2026. Each site has a delineated upstream drainage basin. Features are aggregated over basin cells in distance buckets from the outlet.

## THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET - judge every recommendation against this
The shipped product takes an ARBITRARY MAP PIN anywhere in Iowa, delineates its upstream basin on the fly via USGS NLDI, builds features from weather and land use alone, and predicts daily violation probability. There is NO nitrate history at the target location, NO discharge gauge there, and NO guarantee of a monitored neighbor upstream. Any method that requires the target site's own observations, or requires a gauged upstream site, DOES NOT WORK for this product - it may still be useful for other purposes, but that limitation must be stated explicitly and prominently.

## Current honest performance (leave-one-basin-family-out, LOFO)
- CLF: AUC 0.820, PR-AUC 0.634 (2.41x lift over base rate), recall 0.524 at 10% false-alarm rate, MCC 0.466, Brier 0.137
- REG: R2 0.328, RMSE 4.36 mg/L
- Deployed at beta=2: recall 0.864, but 59% of alarms are false

## THE CENTRAL PROBLEM: the model cannot rank sites
- within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21
- macro_auc 0.90 vs between_rate_r2 0.24
The project's own summary: "a good timer, a mediocre site-ranker." It captures WHEN nitrate rises at a given site, but fails at the ABSOLUTE LEVEL of an unseen basin. Essentially all remaining headroom is in the between-site term.

## CRITICAL SAMPLE-SIZE CONSTRAINT
The ~85 sites collapse to only 19 INDEPENDENT BASIN FAMILIES under the leak-safe CV (sites whose basins nest and whose records overlap in time are grouped). So learning a site's absolute level is a regression with roughly 19 effective independent units, NOT 160k rows. Any method whose published gains come from hundreds of catchments (e.g. CAMELS with 531-671 basins) must be explicitly flagged as possibly infeasible here.

## Current features (68 for CLF)
9 weather variables x 3 distance buckets (SAME-DAY SCALARS ONLY), 8 CDL crop classes x 3 buckets, 2 nitrogen-surplus x 3 buckets, doy_sin/doy_cos, 4 cross-site nitrate lags (rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1/2/3/5), 5 static (lat, lon, log_basin_area, mean_dist_to_sensor, max_dist_to_sensor).
Top features by permutation importance: rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1, lon, lat, doy_sin, fuel_moisture_1000h. BOTTOM: all daily weather; precip_in_1d is dead last (perm ~0.000).

## KNOWN NEGATIVE RESULTS - do not naively re-propose these
- Lagged weather copies: HURT badly (loso_r2 0.116 -> 0.019)
- Rolling precip / water balance as implemented: worse (lofo_r2 0.013 vs 0.003)
- Broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward in time: much worse (-0.166)
- Rolling (3D/7D) smoothed targets: worse
- Spike / anomaly z-score targets: failed cross-site (lofo_r2 ~ -0.0006)
- Antecedent moisture + rain x surplus interactions: REG a wash, CLF only +0.017 PR-AUC
- Riparian 0-2km bucket: CLF +0.039 PR-AUC but REG worse
- Advective travel-time routing IS ALREADY IMPLEMENTED (weather per distance bucket shifted by median flow distance / 2.1 m/s) and is part of the "lagged weather hurt" failure.
PATTERN: nearly every hydrologically-motivated TEMPORAL feature has failed. The only wins came from geometry and static geography. This strongly suggests the deficit is in BETWEEN-SITE static information, not in temporal dynamics.

## Data present on disk but UNUSED
- discharge/streamflow: only 22 of 85 sites (all USGS, 0.66-0.97 density, up to 18 years). ZERO of the 61 IWQIS sites.
- co-located water chemistry: specific conductance (65 sites), water temp (80), pH (64), dissolved oxygen (64), turbidity + phosphate (61)
- upstream_uid (28 sites) / downstream_uid (40 sites) river-network topology: completely unread
- draining_area (80/85), NHDPlus comid (stored per basin), basin containment graph (used only to build CV folds)

## Known data problems
- Nitrogen surplus (gTREND product) ENDS IN 2017 -> NaN for 68% of training rows
- 16.5% of grid cells lack crop/surplus data; an inner join silently UNDER-COUNTS crop area and N surplus for basins extending outside Iowa (worst for the largest multi-state basins)
- Tile drainage density: known to be the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa, NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet


## Non-negotiable rules for this research

1. RECORD THE SPLIT PROTOCOL FOR EVERY PERFORMANCE NUMBER, AND DO NOT COMPARE NUMBERS ACROSS PROTOCOLS. Random-split results are valid evidence about method behavior and should be reported - researchers using them often have good reasons for their own question. But only SPATIALLY HELD-OUT numbers (leave-one-basin-out, leave-one-region-out, ungauged-basin protocol) are comparable to our LOFO 0.820, because a random split over autocorrelated site-days lets a model memorize a site's level and measures interpolation rather than transfer. When the protocol cannot be determined, say so rather than guessing.
2. REPORT EFFECT SIZES AND SAMPLE SIZES, NOT CONCLUSIONS. "GNNs improve water quality prediction" is worthless. "Recurrent GCN, 456 reaches, 42 monitored, held-out-node RMSE 1.83 vs 2.11 for LSTM" is actionable. Always give the number of catchments/basins/sites used.
3. EVERY DATASET RECOMMENDATION MUST BE OPERATIONAL: exact name, spatial resolution, temporal resolution, coverage years, whether it covers ALL of Iowa AND the multi-state portions of basins, exact URL, access mechanism (API/bulk/FTP), authentication requirement, and license.
4. ACTIVELY HUNT FOR NEGATIVE RESULTS. Seven feature-engineering ablations have already failed on this project. Papers reporting that a technique did NOT transfer are as valuable as successes and are systematically under-published - look in discussion/limitations sections and in benchmark comparison papers.
5. FLAG THE n=19-FAMILIES CONSTRAINT against every recommendation. If a method's evidence base comes from 300+ basins, say so explicitly and assess whether it can work at n=19.
6. ACQUISITION CONSTRAINT: recommend only free/public data, or data obtainable by a reasonable request (e.g. emailing IIHR or Iowa DNR). No paid datasets, no field campaigns, no new sensor deployment.
7. Prefer peer-reviewed literature and authoritative agency sources over blog posts. Give DOIs where they exist.
8. JUDGE EVERYTHING AGAINST THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET: an arbitrary ungauged map pin with no local history. State plainly when a method only works at gauged sites.


## Your assignment: synthesize the findings for angle "River-network structure: graph neural networks vs cheap mass-balance topology features"

### Research question
Does exploiting river-network topology - either graph neural networks over reaches, or explicit upstream-downstream mass balance - improve prediction at UNMONITORED nodes? What network size and monitored-node density do published successes require?

### What a good answer contains
Leading river-network GNN papers (Jia/Kumar et al. process-guided recurrent GCN for stream temperature in the Delaware River Basin; Moshe et al. HydroNets; graph models for water quality) with node counts, monitored fractions, and HELD-OUT-NODE results. A clear statement of whether the reported gain is at UNMONITORED nodes or only at gauged nodes with missing time periods - this distinction decides the whole angle. The incremental-area mass-balance literature (USGS load estimation, SPARROW's routing formulation). A blunt assessment of whether an 85-node, ~40-edge graph can support any of it - including whether the honest answer is "use topology as FEATURES (upstream drainage area, Strahler stream order, distance to confluence, position in network) rather than as an architecture." Note that topology-derived FEATURES are computable at an arbitrary ungauged pin from NHDPlus, whereas upstream-sensor-reading features are not.

### TIER 3 - UNVERIFIED claims
These were extracted from real sources but were NEVER adversarially verified - verification was cut to conserve budget. The characteristic failure mode in this corpus is CONFIDENT OVERREACH FROM THIN EVIDENCE, not fabrication: a claim's conclusion is often right while its stated warrant is wrong, its effect size misattributed, or its split protocol misdescribed.

STRICT RULES for tier 3, which you MUST follow:
- USE them for COVERAGE and LEADS: naming a dataset, a URL, an access route, a candidate attribute, or an angle worth pursuing.
- DO NOT use them as the warrant for any numeric performance figure, any effect size, or the core argument of any recommendation. Those must rest on verified (tier 1) claims.
- Any finding that rests on tier 3 MUST set confidence to "unverified" and say so in the claim text itself.
- If a tier 3 claim contradicts a verified claim, the verified claim wins; note the conflict.

Produce the structured finding set for this angle as JSON.

Merge semantic duplicates. Apply every correction supplied by the verifiers. Rank findings by relevance to the BETWEEN-SITE gap specifically. For each finding give feasibilityAtN19 and worksAtUngaugedPin honestly. Populate "datasets" for every concrete data source, with howToIncorporate written concretely enough to act on - name the feature that would be created and how it would be aggregated to a basin. Populate "uncovered" for any part of the question that produced nothing verifiable - absence of evidence must be reported as absence, never silently dropped. Your "verdict" must state plainly whether this angle is worth pursuing and why.

Output JSON with keys: angle, verdict, findings[] (each: claim, confidence, effectSize, splitProtocol, nBasins, sources[], feasibilityAtN19, worksAtUngaugedPin), datasets[] (each: name, url, resolution, years, access, license, coversMultiState, whyUseful, howToIncorporate, limitations), refuted[], uncovered[].
angleTitle: River-network structure: graph neural networks vs cheap mass-balance topology features

tier3_unverified.claim: In the upper Delaware River Basin (70 stream segments), all deep-learning stream-temperature models degraded ~2.2x when moved from gaged to ungaged locations: 1-day-ahead mean RMSE was 1.45-1.52 degC at gaged sites vs 3.18-3.27 degC at ungaged (spatially held-out) sites. Quote: 'All DL models performed substantially better at gaged locations compared to ungaged locations as mean RMSE ranged from 1.45 to 1.52°C for gaged sites and 3.18 to 3.27°C for ungaged sites.' This is direct evidence that the gaged-vs-ungaged transfer penalty is the dominant error term, matching the sustag project's within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21 gap.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 2.2x RMSE increase at ungaged sites (1.45-1.52 -> 3.18-3.27 degC, 1-day lead); at 7-day lead 1.89-1.99 degC gaged vs 3.26-3.39 degC ungaged
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 70 river segments in one basin; 5-fold spatial CV, 6 test segments held out per fold (2 mainstem, 2 headwater, 2 reservoir-impacted) plus 3-4 validation segments

tier3_unverified.claim: The spread across ALL four deep-learning architectures (LSTM, LSTM-DA, RGCN, RGCN-DA) at spatially held-out ungaged sites was only 0.09 degC (3.18-3.27 degC RMSE, 1-day lead) - i.e. the choice of architecture, INCLUDING whether river-network graph structure was used at all, mattered ~25x less than the gaged/ungaged distinction (1.7 degC). This is a strong negative result for the premise that a graph architecture is what unlocks unmonitored-node prediction.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Architecture spread 0.09 degC vs gaged/ungaged gap ~1.73 degC
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 70 river segments, 5-fold spatial CV

tier3_unverified.claim: The graph model did NOT win overall: 'Of the DL models, the LSTM model was generally the best performing model when considering all temperature observations' - the plain LSTM, which uses no river-network topology whatsoever, had the lowest RMSE across both gaged and ungaged locations at 1- and 7-day lead times in the validation period. RGCN/RGCN-DA only won on the >18 degC subset. Therefore the headline 'RGCN-DA is best for ungaged locations' applies to a CONDITIONAL SUBSET (high temperatures), not to overall accuracy.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: LSTM best overall; RGCN/RGCN-DA best only on the >18 degC observation subset
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 70 river segments, 5-fold spatial CV

tier3_unverified.claim: Uncertainty estimates collapsed at unmonitored sites: 90% confidence intervals contained the observation only ~60% of the time at ungaged locations vs ~90% at gaged locations. Models trained on monitored sites are systematically OVERCONFIDENT when applied to unmonitored ones. Directly relevant to the sustag deployment target (arbitrary map pin, beta=2 alarm threshold, 59% false alarms): any calibrated probability produced under LOFO should be assumed miscalibrated at a truly novel pin unless separately validated.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 90% CI empirical coverage ~60% ungaged vs ~90% gaged
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 70 river segments, 5-fold spatial CV

tier3_unverified.claim: The data-assimilation component of this paper requires observations at or near the target site to update model states via an Ensemble Kalman Filter, and the paper's own mechanism for ungaged benefit is that DA lets the network 'borrow information from nearby monitored sites.' This mechanism is UNAVAILABLE at the sustag deployment target, which has no nitrate history at the pin and no guaranteed monitored upstream neighbor. The RGCN-DA ungaged gain is therefore conditional on a dense, hydrologically connected monitored neighborhood (70 segments in a single basin), not on topology features alone.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Not separately quantified; paper does not report the isolated RMSE reduction attributable to DA at ungaged sites
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 70 river segments in one contiguous basin (upper Delaware)

tier3_unverified.claim: The RGCN's graph advantage was network-topology-specific and could be NEGATIVE where topology is complicated: 'RGCN-DA forecasts were worse for locations directly downstream from reservoirs' at gaged locations. The graph adjacency encodes advective connectivity, and where a physical structure breaks that assumption the graph prior hurts. Iowa analogue: tile drainage and impoundments would similarly break a pure NHDPlus flow-topology adjacency, and tile drainage density is already flagged as the dominant unmodeled Iowa control.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Qualitative — direction stated (worse), magnitude not quantified in accessible text
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 70 river segments; 2 of 6 held-out test segments per fold were reservoir-impacted

tier3_unverified.claim: The survey identifies only THREE studies using GNNs for water-resources time-series prediction at unmonitored sites (Sun et al. 2021a; Jia et al. 2021b; Bao et al. 2021), opening the paragraph with 'A few studies use GNNs for prediction in unmonitored sites for water resources applications.' None of the three is a water-quality/nutrient application - two are stream temperature, one is streamflow. The survey reports NO quantitative held-out-node error metrics (no RMSE/NSE numbers) for any of them, only directional statements. FALSIFIABLE: there is no published GNN result in this survey demonstrating a quantified gain for nutrient/nitrate prediction at a held-out node.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: no quantitative metrics reported in the survey for any of the three GNN studies
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 3 GNN studies total; 530 basins (Sun et al. 2021a), 42 river segments (Bao et al. 2021, Delaware River Basin), unstated for Jia et al. 2021b

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT, the strongest in the source: in Sun et al. (2021a) on FIVE HUNDRED AND THIRTY CAMELS basins (daily streamflow), two of the three GNN architectures tested were WORSE than a plain LSTM. Survey text: 'They found that for the transductive case, both ChebNet-LSTMs and GCN-LSTM performed worse in terms of median performance across basins than the standard LSTM and GraphWaveNet was the only one that performed better.' GraphWaveNet (the only inductive-capable model) also beat LSTM in the inductive case. Elsewhere the survey characterizes the GNN advantage as marginal: the graph approach 'can SLIGHTLY outperform the concatenated input approach (Sun et al., 2021a).' At n=530 basins the median GNN gain was slight and 2 of 3 architectures lost outright.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 2 of 3 GNN architectures BELOW standard LSTM in median performance across basins; the one winner described as only 'slightly' outperforming direct-concatenation baseline; no numeric NSE/RMSE given in survey
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 530 basins (CAMELS, USA)

tier3_unverified.claim: The Sun et al. (2021a) graph was NOT river-network topology: 'In all cases, the graph is initially constructed as an adjacency matrix containing the pairwise Euclidean distance between stream sites using site characteristics.' The survey then makes an explicit design criticism of exactly this construction: 'Relying solely on the characteristics or location for graph construction in the non-interacting case more easily allows for broad-scale modeling because it can model spatially disconnected entities, however, it INTRODUCES NO NEW INFORMATION (e.g., physical connectivity) BEYOND WHAT' is already in the characteristics. The survey states that graphs built from real physical connections 'has so far only been seen in stream modeling using stream network graphs (Bindas et al., 2020; Jia et al., 2021b; Moshe et al., 2020; Sit et al., 2021).' IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT: a similarity-graph GNN over 85 sites is provably redundant with static site features already concatenated into XGBoost; only a true upstream-downstream connectivity graph would add information, and our topology covers only 28 upstream_uid / 40 downstream_uid links.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: qualitative design claim; no numbers
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 530 basins (Sun et al. 2021a)

tier3_unverified.claim: The true river-network-topology GNN work is at a network size COMPARABLE TO OURS, not at hundreds of nodes: the survey's Table 1 lists the PDE-driven/knowledge-guided recurrent graph network study (Bao et al. 2021, Delaware River Basin, stream temperature) as covering 'FORTY-TWO RIVER SEGMENTS IN THE DELAWARE RIVER BASIN.' This is the same order of magnitude as our 85 sites / ~40 topology edges, which undercuts the assumption that river-network GNNs require CAMELS-scale samples. HOWEVER the survey reports no node-level error numbers, does not state how many of the 42 segments were monitored, and does not state whether evaluation held out NODES or TIME PERIODS.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: survey states only that the approach improves 'beyond existing process-based and ML approaches'; no RMSE, no monitored-node count, no split design given
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 42 river segments (Delaware River Basin)

tier3_unverified.claim: CRITICAL AMBIGUITY THE SURVEY LEAVES UNRESOLVED FOR THE CENTRAL QUESTION 'unmonitored node vs missing time period': the survey describes Jia et al. (2021b) as taking 'a spatiotemporal GNN approach for stream temperature TEMPORAL PREDICTIONS' - i.e. worded as prediction in time, not at held-out nodes - and reports its result only as: pre-training on PRMS-SNTemp process-model simulations 'outperformed both a non-pre-trained GNN and a baseline LSTM model,' with no metric values. More broadly the survey warns that ALL models in its scope are validated on proxies: 'for evaluation purposes, these models are often tested on PSEUDO-UNMONITORED SITES, where data is withheld until the testing stage to mimic model building for real unmonitored sites.' FALSIFIABLE CONSEQUENCE: this survey does not establish that any river-network GNN gain has been demonstrated at genuinely unmonitored nodes with a quantified effect size.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: no numeric result reported; gain stated only as 'outperformed' a non-pre-trained GNN and an LSTM
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown for Jia et al. 2021b

tier3_unverified.claim: DEPLOYMENT BLOCKER stated explicitly: transductive GNNs (ChebNet-LSTM, GCN-LSTM) require that 'both training and testing entities must be present in the graph' at training time, and 'introducing new test nodes in the graph can affect how information is diffused' prior to re-training; only INDUCTIVE GNNs 'are able to continuously predict on new test data without the need for re-training.' In Sun et al. (2021a) the only architecture that beat LSTM (GraphWaveNet) is also the only inductive-capable one. For an arbitrary Iowa map pin - a node absent from the training graph - every transductive GNN in this survey is architecturally disqualified, and the survey's own evidence is that transductive GNNs were the ones that LOST to a plain LSTM at n=530.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: architectural constraint; transductive variants both below LSTM median, inductive-capable variant above
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 530 basins (Sun et al. 2021a)

tier3_unverified.claim: DIRECT EVIDENCE AGAINST TRAINING ON A SMALL HOMOGENEOUS SET (our n=19 families): 'in Willard (2023), regional LSTM models of stream temperature in the United States perform worse than the LSTM model built on all sites in the CONUS FOR 15 OUT OF 17 REGIONS, and single-site trained models transferred to the testing sites generally performed worse except when pre-trained on the global model.' The survey also cites 'A recent opinion piece Kratzert et al. (2024) also make an argument against building deep learning models, specifically LSTM models, on streamflow data from SMALL HOMOGENEOUS SETS OF WATERSHEDS, ESPECIALLY FOR PREDICTING UNMONITORED AREAS AND FOR EXTREME EVENTS.' A 19-family Iowa-only training set is precisely the small homogeneous regional set these results warn about; the implied remedy is to pool with out-of-state sites (e.g. multi-state Upper Mississippi nitrate networks) rather than to add architecture.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: regional models worse than pooled CONUS model in 15/17 regions (88%); no RMSE values given in survey
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 17 CONUS regions vs 1 CONUS-wide pooled model (Willard 2023, stream temperature)

tier3_unverified.claim: THE MASS-BALANCE / SPARROW HALF OF THE RESEARCH QUESTION IS ABSENT FROM THIS SOURCE. Searching the full text for 'SPARROW', 'mass balance', 'incremental area', and 'load estimation' returns nothing on routed nutrient mass balance; the only routing citation is Bindas et al. (2020), 'Routing flood waves through the river network utilizing physics-guided machine learning.' Mass conservation appears only abstractly, as a candidate knowledge-guided LOSS TERM: 'knowledge-guided loss function terms can impose structure on the solution search space in the absence of labeled target data by forcing model output to conform to physical laws (e.g., conservation of energy or MASS),' with cited successes in lake temperature (Read et al. 2019), lake phosphorus via a power-scaling law (Hanson et al. 2020), and subsurface transport (He et al. 2020) - none at unmonitored river nodes. Also note the water-quality literature for unmonitored sites is thin in this survey: of 40 tabulated studies, the water-quality entries are Kalin et al. (2010) (8 river WQ variables), Noori et al. (2020) (3 nutrient loads, MONTHLY, SWAT output fed to an ANN), and Zhi et al. (2021) (daily dissolved oxygen, 236 CAMELS watersheds); nine of the 40 use CAMELS (671 catchments), and 27 of 40 are US-based.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: absence of coverage; no SPARROW or incremental-area mass-balance literature reviewed
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 40 studies tabulated; 9 use CAMELS (671 catchments); Zhi et al. 2021 uses 236 CAMELS watersheds

tier3_unverified.claim: The entire study is a subset of the Delaware River Basin with exactly 42 river segments (segment lengths 48-23,120 m, each split to ~1 day water travel time, defined by the National Hydrologic Model geospatial fabric), daily data Oct 1 1980 - Sep 30 2016. Water temperature observations existed for 32 of 42 segments (51,103 observations total, 1 to 9,810 per segment) and streamflow observations for 18 of 42 segments (206,920 observations, 4,877-13,149 per segment). Monitored fraction is therefore 76% of nodes for temperature and 43% for flow - an ENORMOUSLY denser monitoring than an arbitrary Iowa map pin, and node count (42) is the same order as our 85 sites / 19 independent families, so this paper is NOT evidence that GNNs need hundreds of basins. It is, however, evidence that they need most of the graph to be gauged.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a - dataset description
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 42 river segments in 1 basin (Delaware River Basin subset); 32 temp-monitored, 18 flow-monitored

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper's headline result ('33%/14% improvement over the state-of-the-art physics-based model and 24%/14% over LSTM ... using very sparse (0.1%) observation data') is measured under a TEMPORAL holdout, not a spatial one: all ML models are global, trained on data from the first 24 years (Oct 1 1980 - Sep 30 2004) and tested on the next 12 years (Oct 1 2004 - Sep 30 2016) AT THE SAME SEGMENTS. The '0.1%' sparsity is a random subsample of labeled site-days within the training period, i.e. sparsity in TIME at already-monitored nodes, not sparsity in SPACE. Exact temperature RMSE at 0.1% labels: PRMS-SNTemp 3.661, ANN 3.706+/-0.114, RNN 3.234+/-0.057, RNNptr 2.818+/-0.059, RGrN 2.849+/-0.049, PGRGrN_ptr 2.556+/-0.045, PGRGrN_ptr,ctr 2.464+/-0.105. At 100% labels the graph advantage nearly vanishes: RNN 1.546+/-0.045 vs PGRGrN_ptr,ctr 1.402+/-0.034 (9%). Streamflow at 100%: RNN 4.406+/-0.064 vs PGRGrN_ptr,ctr 4.076+/-0.059 (7.5%). This headline number is NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820 and must not be cited as ungauged-basin evidence.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Temp RMSE degC at 0.1% labels: RNN 3.234 -> PGRGrN_ptr,ctr 2.464 (-23.8%); at 100% labels RNN 1.546 -> 1.402 (-9.3%). Flow RMSE cms at 100%: RNN 4.406 -> 4.076 (-7.5%)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 42 segments (32 temp / 18 flow monitored)

tier3_unverified.claim: The only genuinely spatial-holdout experiment (Section V-C, 'Assessing performance on unobserved segments') covers just FIVE segments (Seg A-E), each held out one at a time by deleting that segment's training-period observations while all other segments keep theirs, then scoring only on that segment during the 2004-2016 test period. Temperature RMSE (degC), With Obs -> Without Obs: Seg A RNN 2.297->3.328, RGrN 2.135->2.749, PGRGrN_ptr,ctr 2.084->2.501; Seg B RNN 1.116->1.384, PGRGrN 1.047->1.205; Seg C RNN 1.082->1.804, PGRGrN 0.989->1.589; Seg D RNN 0.955->1.805, PGRGrN 0.996->1.297; Seg E RNN 1.067->1.646, PGRGrN 1.013->1.345. So the graph+physics model beats the segment-agnostic RNN at the held-out node in 5/5 temperature cases, by 8% to 28% RMSE - a REAL but modest ungauged-node gain, demonstrated on n=5 nodes with no confidence intervals across nodes.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 5 held-out segments, one at a time, within a 42-segment network

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT, directly on point for our deployment target: for STREAMFLOW the graph architecture made the held-out (unobserved) segment WORSE than a plain RNN at the one headwater tested. Seg A streamflow RMSE Without Obs: RNN 0.879+/-0.063 vs RGrN 1.271+/-0.035 - the graph model is 45% WORSE. The authors explain: 'Seg A is a head water and has no upstream river segments. Hence, the graph convolution is not helpful for modeling Seg A. Besides, the information propagated from neighbors may not always be helpful if neighboring segments have very different streamflow patterns.' Only adding physics pre-training plus the contrastive loss (PGRGrN_ptr,ctr, 0.785) recovered and beat the RNN. Also note RGrN alone barely helps at other held-out flow nodes (Seg C 2.151 RNN -> 2.139 RGrN; Seg E 11.828 RNN -> 12.078 RGrN, i.e. worse). Conclusion: the graph term buys nothing at a node with no gauged upstream neighbor, which is precisely the arbitrary-Iowa-map-pin case.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Seg A held-out streamflow RMSE (cms): RNN 0.879 vs RGrN 1.271 (+44.6% worse); PGRGrN_ptr,ctr 0.785 (-10.7% vs RNN). Seg E: RNN 11.828 vs RGrN 12.078 (+2.1% worse)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 5 held-out segments within 42-segment network; the headwater case is n=1

tier3_unverified.claim: Removing a segment's own observations degrades error at that segment substantially even for the best model, quantifying the irreducible ungauged-node penalty: PGRGrN_ptr,ctr temperature RMSE rises from 2.084 to 2.501 (Seg A, +20%), 0.989 to 1.589 (Seg C, +61%), 0.996 to 1.297 (Seg D, +30%); the plain RNN degrades far more (Seg D 0.955 -> 1.805, +89%; Seg C 1.082 -> 1.804, +67%). The paper states plainly: 'We can observe larger errors produced by all the three models after we remove training data for a segment. This is expected because segment-specific observation data has not been used for refinement of the model.' Also: 'for unobserved river segments, the performance of pre-trained ML models can be no better than physics-based models that can have rather poor performance.' This is independent confirmation of our project's central problem - the between-site absolute level is what is lost when a site's own history is unavailable - and confirms that network topology only PARTIALLY substitutes for it.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Best model's own-observation removal penalty on temperature RMSE: +20% to +61% (median ~+30%); RNN penalty +24% to +89%
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 5 held-out segments within a 42-segment network

tier3_unverified.claim: The ungauged-node gain in this paper is NOT attributable to graph topology alone - it depends critically on a calibrated process model providing dense simulated targets everywhere. The method pre-trains on PRMS-SNTemp (Precipitation-Runoff Modeling System + Stream Network Temperature Model, 84 parameters) simulations assumed available 'on every single date from Oct 01 1980 to Sep 20 2016' at every segment, and additionally uses PRMS-SNTemp INTERNAL VARIABLES (shade fraction, solar radiation, potential evapotranspiration) as 6 of the 10 model input features. Removing pre-training (RGrN alone) is what produces the held-out-node failures above. Separately, the authors' own assessment of the other leading river-network GNN, HydroNets (Moshe et al.), is a documented limitation: 'This method focuses on predicting basins that are well monitored and it remains limited in generalizing to different scenarios or learning with less data.' Implication for our project: there is no calibrated, publicly runnable process model for Iowa daily stream NITRATE that could supply the equivalent dense pre-training signal, so the transferable ingredient here is unavailable to us; the residual, cheap, deployable ingredient is topology as STATIC FEATURES (upstream drainage area, stream order, network position, distance to confluence), which NHDPlus supplies at an arbitrary ungauged pin, unlike upstream-sensor-reading features.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Pre-training contribution at 0.1% labels, temperature: RGrN 2.849 -> PGRGrN_ptr 2.556 (-10.3%) -> PGRGrN_ptr,ctr 2.464 (-13.5% vs RGrN). Streamflow: RGrN 6.299 -> PGRGrN_ptr 5.824 (-7.5%)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 42 segments (Delaware River Basin subset); HydroNets comparison basin count not given in this paper

tier3_unverified.claim: HydroNets was evaluated ONLY at gauged nodes under a TEMPORAL holdout, never at held-out ungauged nodes. The dataset covers five monsoon periods (Jun-Oct) 2014-2018; the paper states 'We used the first four years for training and the last one for testing.' Every node in the graph is a Central Water Commission gauge with its own water-level record, and each node's model is fit to that node's own labels. There is no leave-node-out, spatial-holdout, or ungauged-basin experiment anywhere in the paper. Therefore HydroNets provides ZERO published evidence that river-network architecture helps at an unmonitored node, which is exactly the deployment target of an arbitrary Iowa map pin.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a - protocol claim
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 52 gauged basins total (39 Brahmaputra + 13 Ganga), across 2 regions in India

tier3_unverified.claim: HydroNets requires the target basin's OWN past gauge readings as model input, disqualifying it for prediction at a location with no sensor. The paper states the temporal feature vector 'can include features such as precipitation, temperature, past readings of the gauge itself', and in the experimental setup: 'Every example (i.e., timestamp) in the dataset contains a historical window of length T of the precipitation and past water-levels as the features, and the measurement at t+h as the label.' Additionally, the headline metric R2-persist is defined against a persistence baseline 'that always predicts the future using the present reading of the target label measurement (i.e., y_hat_i^{t+h} = y_i^t)' - a baseline that is undefined at a site with no observations. Both the method and its evaluation metric presuppose a gauged target.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a - input-requirement claim
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 52 gauged basins

tier3_unverified.claim: The per-basin gain of the river-network architecture over a flat (structure-free) linear baseline is small at typical basins and is driven by a handful of outliers. Over all 39 Brahmaputra basins the mean R2-persist improvement is +0.049, but excluding the three largest outliers (Dibrugarh -0.440 -> 0.223 = +0.663; Dholabazar -1.365 -> -1.118 = +0.247; Bhalukpong -0.055 -> 0.163 = +0.218) the mean drops to +0.022. Over all 13 Ganga basins the mean is +0.070, dropping to +0.021 after excluding Kora (-0.542 -> -0.053 = +0.489) and Chillaghat (0.552 -> 0.735 = +0.183). Median improvements are on the order of +0.01 to +0.03 R2-persist. The largest gains occur precisely at basins where the baseline had NEGATIVE skill, i.e. the architecture mainly rescues catastrophic failures rather than improving already-working sites.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Brahmaputra mean diff +0.049 (+0.022 excluding 3 outliers); Ganga mean diff +0.070 (+0.021 excluding 2 outliers); median ~+0.01 to +0.03 R2-persist
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 39 Brahmaputra + 13 Ganga = 52 gauged basins

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT: the river-network architecture made predictions WORSE at 12 of 52 basins (23%). Brahmaputra basins with negative diff: Bihubar (-0.003), Chenimari (-0.019), Chouldhowaghat (-0.001), Margherita (-0.011), Naharkatia (-0.009), Nanglamoraghat (-0.008), Numaligarh (-0.006), Tezpur (-0.056), Tezu (-0.010) - 9 of 39. Ganga basins with negative diff: Hamirpur (-0.002), Shahijina (-0.006), Udi (-0.002) - 3 of 13. The paper's own framing is hedged: 'HydroNets outperforms the flat linear model in a large majority of cases, and provides comparable performance in the rest.' The largest single degradation (Tezpur, -0.056) is larger in magnitude than the median improvement.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 12/52 basins degraded; worst -0.056 R2-persist (Tezpur); median improvement only +0.01 to +0.03
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 52 gauged basins (12 degraded)

tier3_unverified.claim: HydroNets used NO static catchment attributes and only LINEAR sub-models, meaning the paper contains no evidence at all about the between-site / absolute-level problem. The paper states explicitly: 'Note that our implementation of HydroNets (and the baseline) does not include static features' and 'we instantiated HydroNets such that all sub-models are linear.' Adding static basin features is listed only as future work: 'Future work may include non-linear and recurrent sub-models, experimenting in other regions, working with discharge as the label and adding static basin features to the implementation.' The mechanism by which HydroNets gains skill is therefore propagation of upstream GAUGE-DERIVED temporal embeddings downstream - a purely temporal, observation-dependent mechanism, not a static/geographic one. This is directly opposed to the Iowa project's diagnosis that its deficit is in between-site static information rather than temporal dynamics.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a - architecture/ablation claim
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 52 gauged basins

tier3_unverified.claim: The claimed benefit of HydroNets is sample-complexity reduction in a DENSE, FULLY GAUGED tree, not transfer to new locations - and the density requirement is far beyond the Iowa project's 85 nodes / ~40 known edges. The two study regions pack 39 and 13 gauges into single contiguous river trees (every node gauged, in-degree>=1 for most non-leaf nodes), and gains grow as training data shrinks ('HydroNets has a substantial and increasing advantage over the flat linear baseline when the training set becomes smaller', from 4 years down to 1 year of monsoon data). Experiment 1 shows the flat baseline degrades with tree depth while HydroNets 'keeps leveraging information from deeper branches' - a gain that exists only because deeper branches contain MORE GAUGES. The paper's related work confirms the contrasting regime: Kratzert et al. (2019) is described as 'a regional model for hundreds of gauged basins that strongly depends on basin-specific static features', and Shalev et al. (2019) is noted as working 'in the fully gauged setting' with a learned site embedding - a site embedding that cannot be learned for an unseen pin.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Advantage over flat baseline increases monotonically as training years reduced from 4 to 1 (Fig. 5, basins Golaghat, Neamatighat, Chillighat)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 39-node and 13-node fully gauged river trees; contrasted with Kratzert et al. 2019 at 'hundreds of gauged basins'

tier3_unverified.claim: HydroNets was evaluated with a TEMPORAL holdout only, never a spatial/ungauged holdout: the dataset covers five monsoon periods (June-October) 2014-2018, with 'the first four years for training and the last one for testing.' Every basin evaluated in the results tables is a gauged basin that was also present during training. The paper contains no leave-one-basin-out, held-out-node, or ungauged-basin experiment of any kind. Therefore its reported gains are gains at GAUGED nodes over held-out time periods, not gains at unmonitored nodes.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: N/A - this claim is about protocol, not effect size
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 52 gauged basins total (39 Brahmaputra + 13 Ganga), all seen in training

tier3_unverified.claim: HydroNets' architecture is structurally incapable of predicting at a node absent from the training graph. Each node Hi contains three sub-models, two of which are BASIN-SPECIFIC and have per-node parameters: the combiner FiCMB (which fuses upstream embeddings with static features) and the prediction head FiPRD (which emits the target label). Only the middle 'shared hydrologic model' F_SHA has weights shared across basins. A new ungauged map pin has no trained FiCMB or FiPRD, so the published architecture provides no mechanism to instantiate it. Additionally the paper states 'our implementation of HydroNets (and the baseline) does not include static features' - the only route by which an unseen basin could be parameterised is explicitly absent from the tested model.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: N/A - architectural claim

tier3_unverified.claim: HydroNets uses the target gauge's own past observations as an input feature, at every node. The paper states the temporal feature vector 'can include features such as precipitation, temperature, past readings of the gauge itself,' and the empirical setup confirms 'Every example (i.e., timestamp) in the dataset contains a historical window of length T of the precipitation and past water-levels as the features, and the measurement at t+h as the label.' The reported metric R2-persist is defined against a persistence baseline that predicts y_hat(t+h) = y(t), i.e. the model is scored on how much it beats simply repeating the site's own current reading. Both the inputs and the evaluation therefore presuppose a live sensor at the prediction location.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: N/A - input-specification claim

tier3_unverified.claim: Across all 52 basins, HydroNets' gain over a flat linear baseline (which concatenates the same features without using river structure) is small at most sites and concentrated in a few sites where the baseline had catastrophically failed. On the Brahmaputra (39 basins) HydroNets improved R2-persist at 29 basins, tied at 1, and was WORSE at 9; typical improvement was +0.01 to +0.03 (e.g. Dhubri 0.855 -> 0.865, Goalpara 0.851 -> 0.861, Guwahati 0.886 -> 0.911). The headline gains came from basins where the linear model was below zero: Dibrugarh -0.440 -> 0.223 (diff +0.663), Jiabharali -0.014 -> 0.182 (+0.196), Bhalukpong -0.055 -> 0.163 (+0.218), Dholabazar -1.365 -> -1.118 (+0.247). On the Ganga (13 basins) 10 improved, 3 got worse; largest gains Kora -0.542 -> -0.053 (+0.489) and Chillaghat 0.552 -> 0.735 (+0.183); worst regressions Shahijina -0.006, Hamirpur -0.002, Udi -0.002. Results averaged over 10 random initializations.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Median diff ~+0.02 R2-persist; 39/52 improved, 12/52 worse, 1 tie; max +0.663 at a site where baseline was -0.440
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 52 (39 Brahmaputra, 13 Ganga)

tier3_unverified.claim: HydroNets demonstrates that river-structure priors can be exploited at SMALL network sizes - 39 and 13 nodes respectively - rather than requiring the hundreds of catchments used by CAMELS-scale LSTM work. The paper explicitly frames this as the mechanism: 'The injection of the river structure prior knowledge reduces sample complexity and allows for scalable and more accurate hydrologic modeling even with only a few years of data,' and Experiment 3 shows 'HydroNets has a substantial and increasing advantage over the flat linear baseline when the training set becomes smaller' when trained on 1, 2, 3 vs 4 years (test set fixed to the fifth year). This is a direct counterexample to the assumption that network-structure methods need 300+ basins - but the sample-complexity reduction is in TEMPORAL samples per gauged node, not in the number of independent spatial units, and every node is gauged.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Qualitative from Figure 5 (Golaghat, Neamatighat, Chillighat); gap between HydroNets and flat baseline widens monotonically as training years drop from 4 to 1. Exact numbers only shown as plots.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 39 (Brahmaputra) and 13 (Ganga)

tier3_unverified.claim: The graph depth over which structure helps is shallow and saturates: in Experiment 1, when predicting at the region drain basin using upstream trees of increasing depth, 'initially both models gain from deepening the tree but while the baseline model starts deteriorating, the HydroNets model keeps leveraging information from deeper branches.' The flat baseline was fixed at depth 2 for all subsequent experiments 'following our previous experiment,' indicating depth 2 was the optimum for the non-structural model. All HydroNets sub-models in this study were LINEAR; the authors list non-linear and recurrent sub-models, static basin features, discharge as the label, and other regions as UNTESTED future work - so no published evidence exists for HydroNets on a water-quality target, with static catchment attributes, or outside these two Indian regions.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Depth curve reported only as plots (Figure 3, R2-persist; Figure 7, R2); no tabulated numbers
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 2 region drains (one per region), from graphs of 39 and 13 nodes

tier3_unverified.claim: The entire study is a single 42-segment river network — a subset of the Delaware River Basin whose segments feed the mainstream Delaware at Wilmington, DE, each segment split to be roughly one day of water travel time. Of those 42 nodes, water temperature observations existed for 32 segments (76% monitored; 51,103 observations total, 1 to 9,810 per segment) and streamflow observations for 18 segments (43% monitored; 206,920 observations, 4,877 to 13,149 per segment), over daily data from Oct 1 1980 to Sep 30 2016 (13,149 dates). This is a SMALLER and DENSER-MONITORED graph than the Iowa problem's ~85 sites / 19 independent families, so the n=19 constraint is not automatically disqualifying here — but note the monitored fraction (43-76%) is far higher than what an arbitrary Iowa map pin implies, and the paper explicitly frames its own graph as tiny relative to real basins.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a — dataset description
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 42 river segments, 1 basin (Delaware River Basin subset); 32 segments with temperature obs, 18 with streamflow obs

tier3_unverified.claim: THE HEADLINE NUMBERS ARE A TEMPORAL HOLDOUT, NOT A SPATIAL ONE: all ML models are global and 'trained and applied to all the river segments', training on the first 24 years (Oct 1 1980 – Sep 30 2004) and testing on the next 12 years (Oct 1 2004 – Sep 30 2016). Every test segment therefore appears in training. Temperature RMSE at 100% labels: PRMS-SNTemp 3.661, ANN 1.575±0.035, RNN 1.546±0.045, RNNptr 1.444±0.039, RGrN 1.408±0.068, PGRGrNptr,ctr 1.402±0.034 — i.e. the graph model beats a plain LSTM by only 0.144 degC (9.3%) when data is plentiful. Streamflow RMSE at 100%: PRMS-SNTemp 6.834, RNN 4.406±0.064, RGrN 4.139±0.067, PGRGrNptr,ctr 4.076±0.059 (7.5% over RNN). The abstract's advertised '24%/14% over traditional machine learning' gains are obtained only in the artificially sparse 0.1%-label regime (temperature 3.234 RNN -> 2.464 PGRGrNptr,ctr; streamflow 6.885 -> 5.895), not at full data. These numbers are NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: RGrN vs RNN at 100% labels: temperature RMSE 1.408 vs 1.546 (-8.9%); streamflow 4.139 vs 4.406 (-6.1%). At 0.1% labels PGRGrNptr,ctr vs RNN: 2.464 vs 3.234 temp (-23.8%), 5.895 vs 6.885 flow (-14.4%)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 42 segments (32 temp / 18 flow monitored), 1 basin

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper's only true unmonitored-node evidence is a leave-ONE-segment-out experiment on just 5 segments (Seg A–E), and it shows the graph helps but that ALL models degrade substantially when a segment's own observations are removed. Temperature RMSE (with own obs -> without own obs): Seg A RNN 2.297->3.328 vs PGRGrNptr,ctr 2.084->2.501; Seg C RNN 1.082->1.804 vs PGRGrN 0.989->1.589; Seg D RNN 0.955->1.805 vs PGRGrN 0.996->1.297; Seg E RNN 1.067->1.646 vs PGRGrN 1.013->1.345. So on held-out nodes the graph+physics model beats the per-segment-agnostic RNN by roughly 0.18–0.51 degC (10–28%), but even the best model loses 20–30% accuracy relative to having the site's own history. Critically, the authors state there was 'only one segment in the data set for which we have no training data but sufficient testing data' — the genuinely-ungauged evidence base is a SINGLE node, and the 5-segment ablation is a simulation of ungauged conditions at sites that are in fact gauged.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Held-out-node temperature RMSE, PGRGrNptr,ctr vs RNN: 2.501 vs 3.328 (Seg A), 1.205 vs 1.384 (B), 1.589 vs 1.804 (C), 1.297 vs 1.805 (D), 1.345 vs 1.646 (E). Mean degradation from removing own obs: RNN +0.69 degC, PGRGrN +0.36 degC
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 5 segments held out one at a time out of 42; only 1 genuinely never-observed segment in the whole dataset

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT — the graph architecture ALONE (RGrN, without physics pre-training) made held-out streamflow prediction WORSE than a plain RNN at some nodes and catastrophically worse under cross-segment distribution shift. On held-out Seg A (a headwater with no upstream segments), streamflow RMSE was RNN 0.879±0.063 but RGrN 1.271±0.035 — the graph model was 45% WORSE, because 'graph convolution is not helpful for modeling Seg A' and 'information propagated from neighbors may not always be helpful if neighboring segments have very different streamflow patterns.' Worse, in the spatial-transfer experiment where models were trained only on segments with mean flow >3 m3/s and tested on segments with flow <1 m3/s (2005–2016), RGrN scored RMSE 4.073±0.082 versus RNN 3.012±0.432 — the graph model was 35% WORSE than the non-graph baseline, and only recovered (2.099) once physics pre-training plus the contrastive loss were added. This is directly analogous to the Iowa transfer problem: graph message-passing degrades when the held-out node is unlike its training neighbors.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Streamflow RMSE on low-flow held-out segments: RGrN 4.073±0.082 vs RNN 3.012±0.432 (graph 35% WORSE); PGRGrNptr,ctr 2.099±0.088 recovers. Held-out Seg A: RGrN 1.271 vs RNN 0.879 (graph 45% worse)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 42 segments; held-out low-flow (<1 m3/s) segments trained only on high-flow (>3 m3/s) segments

tier3_unverified.claim: The graph gains are inseparable from a calibrated process-based simulator: the best-performing variants (PGRGrNptr, PGRGrNptr,ctr) require PRMS-SNTemp (Precipitation-Runoff Modeling System coupled to Stream Network Temperature Model, 84 parameters) to be run on every date at every segment from 1980–2016 to generate BOTH pre-training targets AND three of the ten input features (shade fraction, solar radiation, potential evapotranspiration), which the authors admit 'are difficult to measure frequently.' Pure RGrN — the architecture-only version obtainable without a simulator — delivered only 1.408 vs RNN 1.546 temperature RMSE at full data and was WORSE than RNN in the two ungauged-transfer settings above. For the Iowa nitrate product, there is no equivalent free, pre-run, per-basin nitrate simulator, so the replicable portion of this paper is the weakest-performing variant.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Architecture-only RGrN vs RNN at 100% labels: 1.408 vs 1.546 temp RMSE (-8.9%); with simulator-based pretraining PGRGrNptr,ctr reaches 1.402 (no further gain at full data) but 2.464 vs RGrN 2.849 at 0.1% labels (-13.5%)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 42 segments, 1 basin

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper's topology encoding is a CHEAP DISTANCE-DECAY WEIGHT, NOT learned structure, and longer routing delays monotonically HURT — both of which support using topology as features rather than as an architecture in the Iowa project. Edges are created wherever segment i is anywhere upstream of segment j, and the adjacency is a closed-form affinity A_ij = 1/(1+exp(dist(i,j))) on standardized along-river outlet-to-outlet distance. In the time-delay ablation (Fig. 7c,d), varying how many days prior the upstream information influences a downstream segment from 1 to 5 steps produced 'a general increase of RMSE when we set a larger time delay' for both temperature and streamflow — i.e. multi-day advective routing degraded performance, matching this project's own finding that travel-time-shifted lagged weather HURT (loso_r2 0.116 -> 0.019). Separately, the authors characterize the main competing river-network GNN, Moshe et al.'s HydroNets, as a method that 'focuses on predicting basins that are well monitored and it remains limited in generalizing to different scenarios or learning with less data' — i.e. HydroNets is NOT evidence for ungauged-node prediction.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Time delay 1 -> 5 days: monotone RMSE increase for both targets (figure only, exact values not tabulated). Adjacency requires only NHDPlus-computable along-network distance, no sensor readings
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 42 segments, 1 basin

tier3_unverified.claim: The primary source PDF (Schwarz, Hoos, Alexander & Smith 2006, USGS Techniques and Methods 6-B3, 248 p.) returned HTTP 403 on every attempted fetch (pubs.usgs.gov PDF, pubs.usgs.gov landing page, and the digitalcommons.unl.edu full-text mirror). Only the bibliographic record was retrievable. All SPARROW claims below are therefore sourced from authoritative USGS secondary pages (water.usgs.gov SPARROW FAQ and USGS 'Everything you need to know about SPARROW') and from peer-reviewed SPARROW applications, NOT from direct reading of tm6b3. Treat quoted figures as second-hand and verify against the PDF before citing.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: source unreachable; 403 Forbidden
tier3_unverified.nBasins: not-applicable

tier3_unverified.claim: SPARROW distinguishes CONDITIONED from UNCONDITIONED predictions: conditioned predictions substitute the OBSERVED monitoring-station load for the model-predicted load on reaches that have a station, so downstream reaches inherit an observation-corrected upstream flux; unconditioned (simulated) predictions use only the model. USGS/RSPARROW guidance states conditioned predictions 'provide the most accurate reach predictions... and reduce the downstream propagation of errors,' but 'unconditioned predictions are most representative of the model skill and performance at monitored and unmonitored stream locations.' DECISIVE FOR THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET: an arbitrary Iowa map pin with no upstream gauge can only ever receive an UNCONDITIONED prediction. Any published SPARROW or mass-balance accuracy figure that is conditioned on observed upstream loads is not achievable at an ungauged pin and must be discarded as evidence for this product.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: qualitative but categorical: conditioned > unconditioned accuracy, by construction, and only conditioned requires upstream observations
tier3_unverified.nBasins: not-applicable

tier3_unverified.claim: SPARROW's core value proposition is exactly the ungauged-prediction problem: it calibrates a nonlinear regression on a few hundred monitored stations and then predicts flux/concentration/yield on a stream network two to four orders of magnitude larger — ERF1 has ~62,000 reaches (1:500K) and NHDPlus has ~2,600,000 reaches (1:100K). The routing is a mass-balance constraint rather than a learned graph architecture: 'contaminant loads coming from upstream as well as those from intervening stream reaches are balanced against the measured downstream load to estimate the amount of instream loss,' with all sources required to be balanced by attenuation losses. This is an EXPLICIT incremental-area mass balance, i.e. topology used as model STRUCTURE with hand-specified decay terms, not as a message-passing GNN, and it requires no observation at the prediction reach.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: ~62,000 ERF1 reaches / ~2.6M NHDPlus reaches predicted; hundreds of calibration stations

tier3_unverified.claim: Published SPARROW calibrations use station counts 10x to 40x larger than this project's 19 independent basin families. The multi-agency regional nutrient SPARROW effort compiled 2,739 monitoring sites from 73 agencies across Major River Basins MRB1-MRB7; per-model counts ranged from 178 sites (MRB7, total nitrogen) to 810 sites (MRB3, total phosphorus), against a network of roughly 240,588 watershed reaches. Reported calibration site density ranged from 0.15 sites/1,000 km2 (MRB4, TN) to 1.09 sites/1,000 km2 (MRB1). No minimum-station or degrees-of-freedom threshold is stated; the emphasis is that 'the range of digital stream-reach network sizes is nearly covered by the range of monitored watersheds,' i.e. representativeness of the calibration set matters more than raw count. FLAG: at n=19 effective independent units, this project sits an order of magnitude below the SMALLEST published SPARROW calibration, so any SPARROW-style regression with more than a handful of free source/decay coefficients is likely overparameterized here.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 2,739 sites total; 178 (MRB7 TN) to 810 (MRB3 TP) per model; ~240,588 reaches

tier3_unverified.claim: SPARROW's reported goodness-of-fit is high but is measured on LOG MEAN ANNUAL FLUX, a quantity dominated by drainage area and discharge, and is an in-sample calibration fit rather than a spatial holdout: USGS states SPARROW models 'explain about 90% of the spatial variability in the log-transformed values of mean annual flux.' A yield-based comparison (USGS SIR 2013-5103, table 8) reports R2 of yield = 0.908 for the NHD-resolution model vs 0.759 for the coarser RF1 model for total nitrogen, and 0.810 vs 0.712 for total phosphorus — evidence that finer network resolution materially improves the area-normalized (between-site level) term. CAUTION: these are calibration-fit R2 values on long-term mean annual aggregates at monitored stations; they are NOT comparable to this project's LOFO daily numbers, and log-flux R2 in particular is inflated by the area/discharge scaling that is trivially predictable.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: ~0.90 R2 on log mean annual flux; yield R2 TN 0.908 (NHD) vs 0.759 (RF1); TP 0.810 vs 0.712
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown (table not directly retrievable; 403)

tier3_unverified.claim: Two structural limits of SPARROW bound how much of it can transfer to this project. (a) TEMPORAL: SPARROW is a steady-state LONG-TERM MEAN ANNUAL model — 'predictions of nutrient sources and loads reflect long-term mean annual nutrient conditions in streams,' standardized to a base year and de-trended to mean flow conditions. It has no daily dynamics at all, so its routing formulation speaks ONLY to the between-site absolute-level term (this project's weak term, between_r2 0.21) and offers nothing for the daily timing term. (b) ACCURACY AT UNGAUGED REACHES IS COARSE: for the 2012 MARB models, 'the prediction accuracy of the mean annual flux in unmonitored reaches is within 55-76% of the mean (RMSE),' described as ~20% lower error than prior SPARROW models. That is a 55-76% relative RMSE on a long-term annual average — a weak bar, and a realistic ceiling estimate for what pure topology-plus-mass-balance buys at an ungauged location.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: unmonitored-reach RMSE 55-76% of the mean, mean annual flux
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown (Robertson & Saad 2021 MARB; article 403, figures via USGS/search summaries)

tier3_unverified.claim: Topp et al. (2023) compared a recurrent graph convolutional network (RGCN) against Graph WaveNet (a temporal-convolution graph model) for daily stream temperature in the Delaware River Basin. When test data were well represented in training, the two architectures were statistically indistinguishable: test RMSE 1.64 °C (Graph WaveNet) vs 1.65 °C (RGCN). Graph WaveNet outperformed RGCN in 4 of 5 experiments whose test partitions represented unseen environmental conditions (including geographic hold-out scenarios). CRITICAL LIMITATION FOR OUR ANGLE: neither the abstract nor any accessible mirror reports a held-out-UNMONITORED-reach RMSE; the headline 1.64/1.65 °C figures are for monitored reaches under a temporal split, and the paper's contribution is XAI-based explanation of *why* one graph architecture generalizes better, not a demonstration that graph structure enables prediction at unmonitored nodes. Full text is paywalled (Wiley returned HTTP 403), so this claim rests on abstract-level metadata.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 1.64 °C vs 1.65 °C RMSE (a 0.01 °C / 0.6% difference — i.e. NO architectural advantage under in-distribution testing); Graph WaveNet better in 4/5 out-of-distribution experiments, magnitudes not available from abstract.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown — Delaware River Basin reach network; the paper's own reach count could not be confirmed from accessible metadata. Associated USGS DRB data releases describe 456 river reaches; the closely related Jia et al. RGCN work used a 42-segment DRB subset.

tier3_unverified.claim: Jia et al. (2021, Physics-Guided Recurrent Graph Networks, IEEE ICDM/arXiv 2009.12575) ran an EXPLICIT held-out-node ablation: they deleted all training observations for one segment at a time (Segs A–E) and evaluated only on that segment during the held-out test period (Oct 2004–Sep 2016). Stream temperature RMSE degraded for every model when the node's own observations were removed, e.g. Seg A: RNN 2.297 -> 3.328 °C, RGCN (RGrN) 2.135 -> 2.749 °C, PGRGrN(ptr,ctr) 2.084 -> 2.501 °C; Seg D: RNN 0.955 -> 1.805, RGrN 0.902 -> 1.597, PGRGrN 0.996 -> 1.297. The graph model's degradation was consistently smaller than the plain RNN's — at Seg D the graph model gave 1.297 °C vs the RNN's 1.805 °C at the unmonitored node, a 28% RMSE reduction. This is the single clearest published evidence that river-network graph structure helps specifically at UNMONITORED nodes, not merely at gauged nodes in held-out time periods.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Unmonitored-node temperature RMSE: 1.297 vs 1.805 °C (Seg D, PGRGrN vs RNN, −28%); 2.501 vs 3.328 °C (Seg A, −25%); 1.205 vs 1.384 (Seg B, −13%); 1.589 vs 1.804 (Seg C, −12%); 1.345 vs 1.646 (Seg E, −18%). Absolute penalty for being unmonitored is large: e.g. Seg C 0.989 -> 1.589 °C (+61%).
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (single-node leave-one-out: target segment's observations removed from training, evaluated on that segment only) combined with a temporal split (train Oct 1980–Sep 2004, test Oct 2004–Sep 2016)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 42 river segments (a subset of the Delaware River Basin feeding the mainstem at Wilmington, DE); only 5 segments (A–E) had enough data to serve as held-out-node test cases

tier3_unverified.claim: Jia et al. (2021) obtained their graph-model gains under EXTREME label sparsity, which is the regime where graph structure pays off: with only 0.1% of labels, DRB stream-temperature RMSE was PGRGrN 2.464 °C vs RNN 3.234 °C vs the physics model PRMS-SNTemp 3.661 °C (a 24% gain over the RNN). With 2% of labels the gain shrank to 1.636 vs 1.908 °C (14%), and with 100% of labels it essentially VANISHED: 1.402 (PGRGrN) vs 1.546 (RNN) vs 1.408 (plain RGrN, no physics guidance) — i.e. graph convolution bought 0.006 °C over its own non-graph-pretrained variant. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT: our Iowa dataset is DENSE, not sparse (160,074 site-days over ~85 sites, near-daily), which is the 100%-label regime where the published graph advantage collapses to noise.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Graph-vs-RNN RMSE gain: 0.770 °C at 0.1% labels, 0.272 °C at 2% labels, 0.144 °C at 100% labels. Graph-vs-nongraph-with-full-data: 1.408 vs 1.546 °C. Streamflow at 100% labels: RGrN 4.139 vs RNN 4.406 — and PGRGrN 4.106, a wash.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (train first 24 years, test next 12 years, all 42 segments; label fraction subsampled at random within the training window)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 42 river segments, Delaware River Basin

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT, directly on-point: Jia et al. (2021) report that the recurrent graph network was WORSE than a plain per-segment RNN at headwater segments, because graph convolution has nothing to aggregate where there are no upstream neighbors. At Seg A (a headwater with no upstream segments), unmonitored-node streamflow RMSE was RGrN 1.271 vs RNN 0.879 — the graph model was 45% WORSE. The authors state verbatim that 'the graph convolution is not helpful for modeling Seg A' and that 'information propagated from neighbors may not always be helpful if neighboring segments have very different streamflow patterns.' This is decisive for an arbitrary-map-pin deployment: most randomly-dropped pins in Iowa land on small headwater catchments with zero monitored upstream neighbors, exactly the case where the published graph architecture underperforms a non-graph model.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Held-out-node streamflow RMSE at headwater Seg A: RGrN 1.271 vs RNN 0.879 (graph model 45% worse); recovered only by adding a contrastive loss (PGRGrN 0.785).
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (held-out node, observations removed) plus temporal split
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 42 segments; the headwater failure case is n=1 segment (Seg A)

tier3_unverified.claim: Zwart et al. (2023, Frontiers in Water, doi:10.3389/frwa.2023.1184992) evaluated RGCN-based water-temperature FORECASTS at 70 locations in the upper Delaware River Basin under a spatial cross-validation design (6 test sites and 3–4 validation sites withheld per fold to simulate unmonitored conditions). At 1-day lead time, RMSE at UNMONITORED locations was 3.18–3.27 °C versus 1.45–1.52 °C at monitored locations — errors roughly DOUBLE at held-out sites. Their data-assimilation variant (ensemble Kalman filter) requires observations at or near the target to update predictions, so its gains are NOT available at a pin with no local sensor. This quantifies the honest ungauged-transfer penalty for river-network graph models and mirrors our own within-site vs between-site gap.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 1-day-lead RMSE 3.18–3.27 °C at unmonitored sites vs 1.45–1.52 °C at monitored sites — a ~2.1x error inflation from spatial transfer.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (spatial cross-validation, 6 test + 3–4 validation sites withheld per fold, simulating unmonitored locations)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 70 locations (monitored and unmonitored) in the upper Delaware River Basin; 6 held-out test sites per fold

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT AGAINST SMALL-GROUP / REGIONAL MODELING, the single most relevant published finding for our n=19-families constraint: a CONUS stream-temperature prediction-in-unmonitored-basins study (arXiv 2410.19865, submitted to Water Resources Research) used 1,362 sites split into 782 training sites (>=5 years of data) and 580 held-out sites (1–5 years of data) treated as 'unmonitored'. A single pooled LSTM trained on ALL sites (LSTM_conus) achieved median per-site RMSE 1.43 °C and had the LOWEST median RMSE in 14 of 17 hydrologic regions and 14 of 15 attribute-similarity clusters, BEATING both regionally-grouped LSTMs and a bottom-up meta-transfer-learning approach. The grouped/regional models collapsed where groups were small: worst-case regional RMSE 9.09 °C (LSTM_regional) and 8.70 °C (LSTM_cluster) in Souris-Red-Rainy, versus 1.43 °C for the pooled model — and the authors attribute this explicitly to 'having very small groups'. No graph/network architecture was needed or used to win. IMPLICATION: with only 19 independent basin families, any method that partitions or specializes by region/cluster is in exactly the failure regime this paper documents; pooling everything into one global model and adding STATIC catchment attributes is what won at scale.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Pooled LSTM_conus median per-site RMSE 1.43 °C vs small-group regional models up to 9.09 °C (6.4x worse) and cluster models up to 8.70 °C; bottom-up MTL worst region 3.58 °C. Adding GAGES-II static catchment attributes dropped median RMSE from 1.78 -> 1.47 °C (−17%); adding river discharge dropped it 1.78 -> 1.57 °C (−12%); combining both reached 1.43 °C. Deep-groundwater-influenced sites had median RMSE 2.00 °C vs 1.26 °C for atmospherically-driven sites.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (782 data-rich sites for training; 580 disjoint data-poor sites held out as 'unmonitored' for final evaluation)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1,362 sites (782 train / 580 held-out unmonitored); an extended Experiment-2 dataset used 2,999 sites with 1,346 training sites
